DPEPO: Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization
for LLM-based Agents

Junshuo Zhang Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Affiliation: DiDi    Chengrui Huang Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Affiliation: DiDi    Feng Guo Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Zihan Li Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Ke Shi Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Menghua Jiang Affiliation: DiDi    Jiguo Yu Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Shuo Shang Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Shen Gao Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents that follow the sequential ‘‘reason-then-act’’ paradigm have achieved superior performance in many complex tasks. However, these methods suffer from limited exploration and incomplete environmental understanding, as they interact with only a single environment per step. In this paper, we first introduce a novel paradigm that enables an agent to interact with multiple environments simultaneously and share cross-trajectory experiences. Building upon this paradigm, we further propose Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that encourages the agent to perform diverse parallel exploration. There are two stages in DPEPO: initial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) imparts basic parallel reasoning and action generation, followed by reinforcement learning stage with a hierarchical reward scheme. We design a parallel trajectory-level success reward and two step-level rewards: Diverse Action Reward and Diverse State Transition Reward, which actively penalize behavioral redundancy and promote broad exploration. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) success rates, while maintaining comparable efficiency to strong sequential baselines.11 1 Code is available at https://github.com/LePanda026/Code-for-DPEPO

1 Introduction

LLM-based autonomous agents commonly adopt the ReAct paradigm Yao et al. (2023), where the agent alternates between reasoning and acting: it selects a single action, observes the environmental feedback, and then uses that observation to inform its next step. This “reason, then act” framework has shown notable success in complex, long-horizon tasks Shridhar et al. (2021); Yao et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2022) by enabling structured, step-by-step reasoning. Recent work Richens et al. (2025) demonstrates that a comprehensive understanding of the environment is crucial for effective and reliable agents. However, ReAct imposes a fundamental limitation: at each step, the agent can perform only one action and observe a single observation. This restricts the breadth of environmental exploration and forces the agent to construct its understanding from a narrow, linear view. As a result, agents often develop an incomplete and biased cognition of the environment, leading to suboptimal decisions and failures in complex tasks.

A straightforward approach to broaden exploration is to sample multiple independent trajectories for the same task. However, this naive multi-sampling strategy faces two critical shortcomings: (1) Lack of diversity: Despite increased output entropy, actions sampled across multiple trials tend to converge to similar choices, failing to promote truly diverse exploration and preventing the agent from developing a comprehensive grasp of the environment. (2) Inefficiency and isolation: Experiences from different trajectories are neither shared nor leveraged, meaning the agent cannot learn from cross-trajectory insights. Moreover, sampling multiple trials sequentially inflates token consumption and running time, making the approach prohibitively costly for practical deployment.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce parallel exploration, a paradigm in which an agent interacts with multiple environments simultaneously. This allows the agent to gather diverse observations in parallel, share experiences across environments, and build a more holistic understanding of the environment dynamics. Building on this exploration paradigm, we propose Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a novel reinforcement learning framework that endows agents with structured parallel exploration capabilities. After an initial SFT phase to acquire basic parallel reasoning and action generation skills, the agent is optimized via a hierarchical reward scheme that encourages diverse exploration at both the trajectory and step levels. Specifically, we design a parallel trajectory-level success reward and two novel step-level rewards: Diverse Action Reward and Diverse State Transition Reward, that actively penalize redundant behaviors. These rewards are combined through a group-relative advantage computation to provide multi-granularity learning signals, enabling the agent to explore more broadly while staying focused on task completion. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, demonstrate that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art success rates across all task splits. Notably, our analysis of trajectory length and token usage reveals that DPEPO achieves efficiency comparable to strong sequential baselines, despite its parallel nature.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

∙\bullet We propose Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a novel RL framework that pioneers parallel exploration for agents to build holistic environment cognition.

∙\bullet We design a Parallel Trajectory-level Success Reward to optimize task completion in concurrent multi-environment settings.

∙\bullet We propose Parallel Step-level Rewards (Diverse Action & State Transition) to penalize redundancy and foster distinct explorations.

∙\bullet Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show DPEPO achieves SOTA performance in terms of success rates while maintaining comparable efficiency with single exploration methods.

2 Related Work

LLM as Autonomous Agents

LLMs are increasingly being deployed as autonomous agents across a wide range of domains, including code generation Zhang et al. (2024), web navigation Abuelsaad et al. (2024), smart device control Zhang and Zhang (2024); Gur et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025b); Ye et al. (2025), external tool use Gao et al. (2024); Shi et al. (2024); Shi et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2025) and interactive gaming Shridhar et al. (2021); Yao et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023). Early LLM-based agents typically relied on engineered prompting strategies Wei et al. (2022) to achieve strong performance, such as ReAct Yao et al. (2023) and Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023). Recent studies has shifted their focus toward fine-tuning LLMs for agent-related tasks using either SFT Song et al. (2024); Xi et al. (2024) or RL Feng et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025), aiming to develop agents with greater generalization ability and robustness, ultimately resulting in more efficient and resilient behaviors compared to earlier prompt-based methods.

Reinforcement Learning for LLM-based Agents

Reinforcement learning has been recognized as a foundational approach for enabling LLMs to operate as autonomous agents in complex environments. Early work in this domain primarily employed PPO Schulman et al. (2017), which allowed agents to learn diverse interactive tasks while avoiding the need for expensive imitation data. With the emergence of reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) Guo et al. (2025); Lambert et al. (2025) and group-based policy optimization Shao et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2025); Kool et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2025c), a series of studies have eliminated complex reward model and critic model, instead adopting rule-based reward signals: GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) proposes anchor state groups to estimate the quality of specific steps; RLVMR Zhang et al. (2025) introduces meta-reasoning and corresponding step-level rewards to address inefficient exploration; iStar Liu et al. (2025a) estimates step rewards via the LLM’s intrinsic implicit rewards. However, these methods remain constrained by the sequential ReAct paradigm, which limits their exploration space and maintains a narrow focus on single-path reasoning. In this work, we introduce a novel reinforcement learning algorithm for training agents with more fine-grained reward shaping, drawing from the insight that more diverse and comprehensive exploration, helping agents build a better understanding of environments, thereby enabling them to perform tasks more effectively.

3 Methodology

In this section, we first introduce the parallel agent exploration framework, and then we detail the framework for training the LLM-based agent to perform parallel exploration. The overall architecture is shown in Figure 2.

3.1 Parallel Agent Exploration Formulation

Given a task specified by a prompt and a set of KK parallel environments ℰ={E1,E2,…,EK}\mathcal{E}=\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{K}\} sharing the same initial state, an LLM-based agent interacts with ℰ\mathcal{E} over multiple turns until the task is completed or the maximum allowed step TT is reached. Specifically, at step tt, the agent selects a subset of all environments ℰt′\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}. Let |ℰt′||\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}| denote the number of selected subset, due to the agent dynamically selects environments to interact, |ℰt′||\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}| can vary at each step. For the selected environments, the agent generates a set of parallel actions At={(Ei,at)∣Ei∈ℰt′}A_{t}=\{(E_{i},a_{t})\mid E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}\}, which are executed simultaneously in their respective environments. The agent then observes the resulting states St={(Ei,st)∣Ei∈ℰt′}S_{t}=\{(E_{i},s_{t})\mid E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}\}. Consequently, the agent’s full trajectory can be denoted as:

τ={(St,At)}t=1T,\tau=\{(S_{t},A_{t})\big\}_{t=1}^{T}, (1)

where the trajectory τ\tau consists a sequence of parallel states and parallel actions.

3.2 Parallel Exploration Capability Cold Start

We begin with an SFT-based cold start stage to endow the agent with foundational skills for structured output and parallel exploration. For the SFT training data, we introduce human prior knowledge into its synthetic pipeline. The data synthesis pipeline is two steps: (1) We first manually annotated five ground-truth trajectories. Each trajectory consists of multiple steps, with some key steps containing two or more parallel exploration actions. (2) Based on these trajectories, we employ DeepSeek-V3.2 to annotate trajectories containing parallel exploration behaviors. Finally, the agent is fine-tuned on these annotated trajectories, learning to imitate the parallel exploration patterns.

Next, we employ a reinforcement learning method to train the LLM to perform better parallel exploration actions by using dual-level rewards as the training signal: trajectory-level and step-level.

3.3 Parallel Trajectory-level Success Reward

In this section, we extend the rule-based success reward to parallel setting. Formally, given a task, parallel environments ℰ\mathcal{E}, agent interaction trajectory τ\tau and task success state 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the parallel trajectory-level success reward is calculated as follows:

Rt​r​a​j​(τ)={1if ​ST∩𝒢≠∅,0,otherwise.R_{traj}(\tau)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }S_{T}\cap\mathcal{G}\neq\emptyset,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2)

This parallel trajectory-level success reward signifies that when any state in STS_{T} reaches a goal state, the overall trajectory is considered successful. This reward provides an important training signal that guides the agent to complete the task.

3.4 Parallel Step-level Rewards

The trajectory-level reward provides an important yet coarse-grained signal, failing to assess individual steps with parallel actions. To provide fine-grained guidance for diverse exploration and better information acquisition, we introduce two novel step-level and diversity-driven rewards: Diverse Action Reward and Diverse State Transition Reward. These rewards discourage redundant exploration behavior, forcing the agent to gather more information for making better decisions. These dense, step-level reward signals complement the sparse trajectory-level reward, together providing a multi-granularity learning signal for parallel agent.

Diverse Action Reward

To incentivize diverse exploration behavior, we define a composite reward that incorporates both depth-wise (within a single environment) and width-wise (across different environments at the same step) considerations.

Formally, at step tt, given the selected environments ℰt′\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime} and generated parallel actions AtA_{t}. We compute this reward as follows:

Raction​(At)=1|ℰt′|​∑Ei∈ℰ​t′αCdepth​(Ei,at)+ωCwidth​(At),R_{\text{action}}(A_{t})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}|}\sum_{E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}t^{\prime}}\alpha^{\,C_{\text{depth}}(E_{i},a_{t})}+\omega^{\,C_{\text{width}}(A_{t})}, (3)

where Cdepth​(Ei,at)C_{\text{depth}}(E_{i},a_{t}) is the number of repetitions of action ata_{t} in environment EiE_{i}, ωCwidth​(At)\omega^{\,C_{\text{width}}(A_{t})} is the number of repeated actions in 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}. The α,ω∈(0,1]\alpha,\omega\in(0,1] are discount factors corresponding to depth-wise and width-wise rewards. The Diverse Action Reward encourages diversity within each environment and between parallel environments.

Diverse State Transition Reward

Beyond individual actions, we further propose the diverse state transition reward to discourage the agent from repeating the same state-action transitions, this reward also operates at both depth and width level.

At step tt, for each environment in selected ℰt′\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}, the agent observes state sts_{t}, takes an action ata_{t}, define this state-action transition as pt=st→atp_{t}=s_{t}\rightarrow a_{t}. The parallel state StS_{t} and parallel actions AtA_{t} result in parallel state-action transition {(Ei,pt)|Ei∈ℰt′}\{(E_{i},p_{t})|E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}\}. We compute this reward as follows:

Rtransition​(At)=1|ℰt′|​∑Ei∈ℰt′γMdepth​(Ei,pt)+1|ℰt′|​∑Ei∈ℰt′βMwidth​(Ei,pt),\begin{split}R_{\text{transition}}(A_{t})=&\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}|}\sum_{E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}}\gamma^{M_{\text{depth}}(E_{i},p_{t})}\\ \quad+&\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}|}\sum_{E_{i}\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\prime}}\beta^{M_{\text{width}}(E_{i},p_{t})},\end{split} (4)

where Mdepth​(Ei,pt)M_{\text{depth}}(E_{i},p_{t}) measures the recurrence of the transition ptp_{t} within the environment EiE_{i}, and Mwidth​(Ei,pt)M_{\text{width}}(E_{i},p_{t}) counts how many other selected environments have previously observed the same transition. The γ,β∈(0,1]\gamma,\beta\in(0,1] are discount factors for the depth-wise and width-wise terms, respectively.

Step-Level Composite Reward

The final reward for step AtA_{t} is the average of Diverse Action Reward and Diverse State Transition Reward:

Rs​t​e​p​(At)=Ra​c​t​i​o​n​(At)+Rt​r​a​n​s​i​t​i​o​n​(At)2.R_{step}(A_{t})=\frac{R_{action}(A_{t})+R_{transition}(A_{t})}{2}. (5)

This reward provides a dense, multi-granularity policy optimizing signal that actively promotes diverse and efficient exploration.

3.5 Policy Optimization

Similar to GRPO Shao et al. (2024), DPEPO eliminates the critic model and instead estimates the advantages of trajectories through group sampling and relative advantage computation. For a given task, we sample a group GG containing NN trajectories {τ}i=1N\{\tau\}_{i=1}^{N}, each trajectory paired with its corresponding trajectory reward Rt​r​a​j​(τi)R_{traj}(\tau_{i}):

G={(τi,Rt​r​a​j​(τi))}i=1N.G=\big\{(\tau_{i},R_{traj}(\tau_{i}))\big\}_{i=1}^{N}. (6)

We then access the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward using group-level statistics:

Φt​r​a​j​(τi)=R⁡(τi)−mean​({Rt​r​a​j​(τj)}j=1N)std​({Rt​r​a​j​(τj)}j=1N).\Phi_{traj}(\tau_{i})=\frac{R(\tau_{i})-\text{mean}\left(\{R_{traj}(\tau_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}\right)}{\text{std}\left(\{R_{traj}(\tau_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}\right)}. (7)

The trajectory-level advantage Φt​r​a​j​(τi)\Phi_{traj}(\tau_{i}) reflects the agent’s overall success in completing the task. Similar to standard GRPO, it performs on outcome-level credit assignment, encouraging policy to develop long-horizon behaviors to complete the task. We use this trajectory-level advantage as the base advantage for more fine-grained, step-level advantage computation. More specifically, at step tt, given a step Ai,tA_{i,t} in trajectories τi\tau_{i} with its associated step reward Rstep​(Ai,t)R_{\text{step}}(A_{i,t}), we compute the step-level advantage by combining this immediate reward with the global trajectory advantage:

Φs​t​e​p​(Ai,t)={Rstep​(Ai,t),if ​Φt​r​a​j​(τi)>0,2−Rstep​(Ai,t),otherwise.\Phi_{step}(A_{i,t})=\begin{cases}R_{\text{step}}(A_{i,t}),&\text{if }\Phi_{traj}(\tau_{i})>0,\\ 2-R_{\text{step}}(A_{i,t}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (8)
Φ⁡(Ai,t)=Φs​t​e​p​(Ai,t)⋅Φt​r​a​j​(τi).\Phi(A_{i,t})=\Phi_{step}(A_{i,t})\cdot\Phi_{traj}(\tau_{i}). (9)

This combined advantage provides hierarchical supervision by assigning credit at both trajectory and step scales, thereby enabling the learned policies to exhibit more diverse behaviors across parallel environments. We then optimize the policy for each step using the same objective as GRPO. The pseudo code for our algorithm can be found in Appendix D.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Datasets

We train and evaluate the LLM-based agents on two challenging benchmarks: ALFWorld Shridhar et al. (2021) and ScienceWorld Wang et al. (2022). ALFWorld is a text-based interactive environment where agents perform everyday household tasks through multi-step reasoning and interactions. It presents goals like “put the pencil on the desk”, requiring agents to explore simulated rooms based on common sense. The environment is fully text-based and only returns a reward signal upon final success or failure. ScienceWorld is a simulated benchmark designed to evaluate scientific agent’s reasoning capabilities across diverse elementary science topics. It includes tasks from 10 domains, including electricity, life cycles, and chemical reactions. Each task consists of multiple intermediate sub-goals that agents must complete sequentially.

4.2 Baselines

For ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, we compare our approach with a range of competitive baselines under the ReAct paradigm: (1) Closed-source LLMs: GPT-4o Hurst et al. (2024), DeepSeek-V3 Liu et al. (2024), and DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025), which show superior performance on various natural language tasks. (2) A series of RL methods: GRPO Shao et al. (2024), which performs advantage estimation over trajectory groups; GiGPO Feng et al. (2025), introducing step-level advantage through anchor state grouping; RLVMR Zhang et al. (2025), which proposes meta-reasoning rewards to address inefficient exploration; and SPEAR Qin et al. (2025), leveraging self-imitation and intrinsic rewards to improve the exploration–exploitation balance.

4.3 Implementation Details

We conduct experiments on various model sizes of Qwen2.5-Instruct Yang et al. (2025b) and Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025a). For cold start training, we annotate approximately 500 and 1,000 for ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, respectively. For reinforcement learning stage, the number of training sample is 500, the temperature for rollout is 0.4, the rollout group size NN is set to 8 for ALFWorld and 4 for ScienceWorld, with 1 epoch and a total of 125 training steps. The max step is 25, and the number of parallel environments is 4. Full hyperparameter details and prompts used for training are provided in Appendix  B and Appendix  C.

5 Experimental Results

5.1 Overall Performance

Table 1 demonstrates the performance of DPEPO and baselines on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld datasets. As illustrated, closed-source LLMs exhibit only limited performance: On ALFWorld, DeepSeek-R1 achieves a success rate of 80.1%, and on ScienceWorld, GPT-4o reaches 45.2%. Under the ReACT paradigm, RL training yields substantial improvements: GRPO raises the average success rate on ALFWorld to 72.0% for the 1.5B model and 77.5% for the 7B model, demonstrating the effectiveness of rule-based success reward. However, the coarse-grained nature of this reward limits further performance gains. In contrast, GiGPO, SPEAR and RLVMR address this issue by incorporating step-level rewards that provide more fine-grained optimization signals for intermediate reasoning steps. Among these methods, RLVMR achieves the strongest performance, with average success rates of 91.6% on ALFWorld and 47.5% on ScienceWorld. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of these RL methods, they remain constrained by the ReAct paradigm, which restricts the breadth of environmental exploration and forces the agent to construct its understanding from a narrow, linear view. Our proposed DPEPO addresses this limitation through parallel exploration and diversity-driven rewards, achieving the best results: 98.2% on ALFWorld and 61.4% on ScienceWorld. It also demonstrates strong generalization on unseen ALFWorld tasks and on the L1 and L2 splits of ScienceWorld. This significant improvement can be attributed to diverse parallel exploration, which allows agents to gain a comprehensive understanding of the environment, thereby supporting more informed decision-making and ultimately leading to more successful task completion.

5.2 Scaling Abilities of DPEPO

In this section, to demonstrate the scaling potential of DPEPO, we present its performance across models with varying model sizes. As shown in Figure 3, DPEPO exhibits consistent performance improvements and higher efficiency as the model size increases, underscoring its generalization and scaling abilities. Moreover, on the ALFWorld benchmark, even our smallest DPEPO variant (based on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) outperforms the strong baseline RLVMR by 2.53% in success rate and completes tasks in fewer steps. On the more challenging ScienceWorld benchmark, DPEPO further achieves higher performance with competitive efficiency. This highlights that diverse parallel exploration enables more effective and efficient task completion. More scaling experiments conducted on Qwen3 series can be found in Appendix A.1.

5.3 Analysis of Environment Numbers

Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying the number KK of parallel environments during inference. For this analysis, we evaluate on both seen and unseen tasks in ALFWorld and report the average success rate. During DPEPO inference, we introduce a limiting prompt that specifies the maximum number of parallel environments the agent is allowed to explore; any trial that exceeds KK is treated as a failure. We use GiGPO with multiple sampling as our baseline; in GiGPO, KK denotes the number of sampled trajectories.

As shown in Figure 4, both DPEPO and GiGPO exhibit stable performance improvement trends as KK increases, but DPEPO consistently outperforms GiGPO across all values of KK. Moreover, DPEPO achieves strong performance even at small KK, demonstrating high sample efficiency. In terms of token usage, the token budget of DPEPO is only slightly higher than that of GiGPO when KK is small. As KK increases, GiGPO’s token consumption increases approximately linearly, while the token budget of DPEPO grows much more slowly. Notably, DPEPO without any restriction on exploration environments not only achieves the best performance, but also explores fewer environments on average. The reason for this phenomenon is that the environmental limit prompt may introduce additional inductive bias, causing the model to explore all environments exhaustively rather than selectively.

5.4 Ablation Study

Next, we conducted an ablation study to evaluate the contribution of each proposed reward component. We compare DPEPO against four variants: the variant only performed the cold start stage (ColdStart), DPEPO without Diverse Action Reward (DPEPO w/o DAR), DPEPO without Diverse State Transition Reward (DPEPO w/o DTR), and DPEPO with neither reward (DPEPO w/o DAR & DTR). As shown in Table 2, the ColdStart variant yields only moderate performance. Removing either DAR or DTR leads to a significant performance degradation, and the variant without both rewards shows an even greater decline. This suggests that DAR and DTR jointly provide training signals for the policy optimization process, thus contributing to the superior performance of DPEPO. More detailed results of specific tasks can be found in Appendix A.2.

To further understand how these reward components influence agent’s behavior, we visualize several exploration metrics across aforementioned variants: (1) exploration diversity, (2) state transition repeat count, (3) action repeat count, and (4) trajectory length. The repetition counts are computed using Equations 3 and  4, exploration diversity is the fraction of unique actions among all actions in parallel trajectories. As illustrated in Figure 5, agents trained with DPEPO exhibit significantly lower action and transition repetition and higher exploration diversity compared to ablated variants. This indicates that the DAR and DTR shape the agent’s policy to generate trajectories that are not only more goal-directed but also more diverse and efficient, thereby achieving a better trade-off between exploration and task success.

5.5 Efficiency Analysis

5.5.1 Inference-time Efficiency Analysis

Having established the effectiveness of our approach in terms of success rate, we now turn to its efficiency: while diverse parallel exploration behavior broadens the search space, it may also lead to a higher computational budget or inference time.

To quantitatively assess this trade-off, We compare the token budget and inference time of DPEPO with those of various methods on ALFWorld. As shown in Table 3, although understanding parallel environments brings higher token budgets, DPEPO completes tasks with significantly shorter trajectories and faster inference time compared to GiGPO and the DeepSeek series. We attribute this to two factors: (1) simultaneously executed parallel actions do not increase inference time, and (2) parallel interaction enables the agent to acquire more comprehensive environmental insights, supporting more purposeful decision-making that leads to more efficient and successful task completion.

5.5.2 Training Efficiency Analysis

We further evaluate the training efficiency of DPEPO in comparison with GiGPO, a critic-free method known for its training efficiency and strong performance. We first compare the time consumption per reasoning step. As shown in the left part of Figure 6 and Figure 7, although our method explores more environments in parallel, the time consumption per step does not increase significantly. Despite the longer time per step, the overall training efficiency of DPEPO is significantly higher: as shown in the right part of Figure 7, including the cold start stage, DPEPO achieves superior final performance in approximately 24 hours using only 500 RL training samples. In contrast, GiGPO requires 96 hours of training to reach its peak performance. This experiment is conducted using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Further details and experimental setup of this experiment are provided in Appendix A.3.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we propose a novel parallel exploration paradigm and reinforcement learning algorithm to address the constrained exploration challenge inherent in ReACT paradigm. We first extend the ReACT framework to enable agents to simultaneously explore multiple parallel environments. We then introduce Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a novel diversity-driven policy gradient algorithm specifically designed for parallel agents. By incorporating fine-grained, step-level rewards into the parallel trajectory-level success reward, DPEPO encourages agents to perform more diverse exploration in parallel environments. Empirical evaluations across all test splits on ALFWorld and the more challenging ScienceWorld benchmarks demonstrate that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art performance and high sample efficiency. Through extensive experiments and analysis, we show that the diverse parallel exploration behavior reinforced by DPEPO leads to superior task performance, higher efficiency, and more effective token usage.

Acknowledgments

This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62432002 and 62406061), the CCF-DiDi GAIA Collaborative Research Funds (CCF-DiDi GAIA 202504), and the State Key Laboratory of Internet Architecture, Tsinghua University (HLW2025MS10).

Limitations

While DPEPO shows significant improvements in performance and efficiency, it still faces challenges in real-world scenarios where parallel environments are hard to build. However, we suggest a possible solution: training agents to complete different tasks in parallel, which might help mitigate this issue in real-world scenarios. We leave this exploration for future work.

Ethical Considerations

In some real-world environments that may contain biases, parallel exploration enables the agent to gather more experience, which could lead it to learn those biases, potentially resulting in unfair or unsafe behavior. Therefore, before applying our proposed method to real-world tasks, developers should conduct thorough evaluations in their target environments to ensure the agent acquires accurate and objective knowledge and performs actions safely and responsibly.

Appendix A Supplementary Results of Experiments

A.1 Additional Results of Scaling Analysis

In Section 5.2, we presented the performance of Qwen2.5 variants across different model scales. Here, we provide a detailed results of Qwen3 variants with varying parameter, reporting their average success rate on both seen and unseen tasks of ALFWorld. Full results are shown in Figure 8. As illustrated, stronger models consistently achieve higher performance. Within the Qwen3 series, success rate improves steadily with model size, demonstrating clear and predictable scaling behavior.

A.2 Detailed Results of Ablation Study

In Section 5.4, we have reported the performance of various DPEPO variants. In this section, we provide a more detailed breakdown of their results across individual tasks in the ALFWorld In-Domain setting. Full scores are shown in Table 4.

A.3 Details of Training Efficiency Analysis

Both our approach and GiGPO are adapted from GRPO and thus follow the same training pipeline as GRPO, which includes multi-turn rollout, old policy probability computation, reward and advantage estimation, and policy updates. We have reported the total training time in Section 5.5.2; in this section, we detail the time consumption of different training components per step.

During DPEPO training, the agent is allowed to explore up to 4 parallel environments per step, with a maximum of 25 steps per trajectory. In contrast, GiGPO explores only a single environment with no more than 50 steps. Under this setting, Figure 6 indicates that although the DPEPO rollout phase takes longer than that of GiGPO due to parallel execution, policy updates, probability recomputation, and advantage estimation are consistently faster. We attribute this to the reduced average trajectory depth under parallel exploration, which yields fewer but higher-quality samples for policy updates.

A.4 Reward Hacking Analysis

Although we do not explicitly penalize over-exploration in the reward design, the inherent context window imposes a practical constraint. Excessive exploration across too many environments causes a rapid increase in context length, and exceeding the context limit is treated as task failure. Additionally, exploring too many environments leads to redundant actions and state transitions. In this situation, the diversity-driven step-level reward naturally penalizes this behavior, which help reduce unnecessary exploration. We further present the training dynamics of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to substantiate above claim. As shown in Table 5, the agent’s exploration behavior remains stable.

A.5 DPEPO’s Performance without ColdStart

A concern may arise regarding the respective contributions of the SFT and RL stages. Therefore, we supply additional ablation results conducted on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under the same setting as GRPO. As shown in Table 6, the variant DPEPO w/o ColdStart still outperforms the GRPO baseline, confirming the effectiveness of DPEPO.

A.6 Comparision with Stronger Baselines

As presented in Table 7, we further added performance comparisons on ALFWorld against stronger baselines, including methods that employ exploration-based strategies and advanced imitation learning approaches. Although basic SFT yields only moderate performance, prompting with advanced exploration strategies like MCTS brings substantial improvements. Furthermore, curating trajectories or preference pairs from MCTS traces to fine-tune the LLM enhances performance even further. Despite these advancements, these methods still lag behind DPEPO and suffer from complex backtracking and expansion operations.

A.7 Parallel Exploration Behavior Analysis

Exploration Strategy

As presented in Figure 9, the agent performs more parallel actions in the early steps. At this stage, the agent is unfamiliar with the environment and relies on parallel exploration to rapidly build a preliminary understanding of task and environment. In the later steps, after acquiring a basic model of the environment and the task, the agent shifts its strategy toward focused exploration. It reduces the number of parallel actions and concentrates on a specific environment, using only a few parallel actions to support its more targeted exploration.

Efficient Search via Parallel Actions

The case shown in Figure 18 illustrates how the agent efficiently searches for a candle that is not visible in the initial observation. Recognizing that candles are commonly stored on shelves, the agent prioritizes the three shelves in the room as likely candidates. Instead of checking them one by one, it leverages parallel environments to visit shelf 1, shelf 2, and shelf 3 simultaneously. This strategy reduces search time and demonstrates the agent’s ability to perform goal-directed exploration by distributing candidate actions across multiple environments.

Validating Hypotheses via Parallel Exploration

As the case shown in Figure 19, when the agent repeatedly fails to take book 2 from the bed, it hypothesizes that there might be a carrying limit. To test this, it uses parallel environments to check its inventory in env_1 and env_2 while also looking around in env_3 to gather more context. This demonstrates the model’s ability to perform reasoning and efficiently validate hypotheses through parallel exploration.

Keep Exploring Even After Finding a Solution

The case in Figure 20 shows that even after finding the mug in environment 4, the agent keeps checking other places in parallel, just in case there’s a better option or something it missed. This shows the model doesn’t stop exploring too early, which helps it make better decisions in uncertain environments.

Structured Search Across Location Types

The case in Figure 21 shows that after failing to find a tomato in the fridge across all environments, the agent, based on common-sense knowledge of where tomatoes might be, systematically uses each parallel environment to explore a different type of location: cabinets, drawers, and countertops. Instead of randomly trying places, it assigns each environment a distinct category to cover more ground efficiently. This demonstrates the DPEPO’s ability to perform structured exploration.

A.8 Applicability of DPEPO Analysis

Although parallelizing interactions remains difficult in embodied agent scenarios, our paradigm is highly applicable to a wide range of dominant current agent scenarios. (1) Code Generation: Agents can compile and test code in isolated, parallel sanboxes to rapidly verify correctness. (2) Tool Learning: Agents mastering multiple tools and APIs can invoke them in parallel to support simultaneous sub-task execution or efficient trial-and-error. (3) GUI Agent: Web or desktop environments can be instantiated simultaneously in multiple headless browsers or virtual machines. (4) DeepResearch Agent: Information seeking tasks naturally support parallel querying across diverse search engines and document sources. We hope these examples illustrate that, though challenges remain in real-world embodied scenarios, our approach still offers a practical and efficient solution for many important agent tasks. We look forward to further exploring how this paradigm might be adapted to broader scenarios in future work.

Appendix B Experimental Details

B.1 SFT Training Details

Datasets

For ALFWorld, we annotate 500 successful trajectories from the training split. For ScienceWorld, we adopt the same data partitioning strategy as RLVMR, which defines three difficulty levels: L0, L1, and L2. For training on L0 and L1, we annotate 1,000 trajectories from the L1 training set (used for both L0 and L1 training for simplicity). Consequently, our model faces a more challenging L0 evaluation compared to RLVMR, as it is trained with fewer L0-specific examples. For L2, we annotate 500 trajectories for training.

Experiment and Hyperparameters Details

All our SFT experiments are conducted using the OpenRLHF framework. Specifically, we employ DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with Adam optimizer offloading enabled. The model is trained with a maximum sequence length of 8,192 tokens, a learning rate of 5e-6, and bfloat16 mixed-precision, with FlashAttention-2 enabled in all experiments. The batch size is set to 4 for ALFWorld and 16 for ScienceWorld.

B.2 RL Training Details

Datasets

For both ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, we select 500 samples from the training set that excludes SFT samples for RL training.

Experiment and Hyperparameters Details

All RL experiments is conducted based on verl-agent framework and Ray-based dirtributed parallel environment. The maximum prompt length is set to 10,240 tokens and the maximum response length to 2,048 tokens, with each trajectory allowed up to 25 environment steps. The final actor learning rate is 1e-6, and we employ parallel trajectory-level reward that awards +1 for task success. Repetition penalties are applied consistently across both environments, with coefficients of 0.8 for depth-level action repetition and 0.95 for width-level action repetition, depth-level transition repetition, and width-level transition repetition. Notably, ScienceWorld includes an additional penalty coefficient of 0.5 for invalid actions, which is not used in ALFWorld. Both environments run with a maximum of 4 parallel exploration trajectories during training. For group-based reinforcement learning, ALFWorld adopts a group size of 8 while ScienceWorld uses a group size of 4; in both cases, 4 distinct groups are sampled per rollout. The rollout temperature is set to 0.4, and the mini-batch size is 32. All policy updates are performed using LoRA, with the LoRA rank and scaling factor are all set to 32.

B.3 Computation Details.

For parallel environments, we cap the maximum CPU usage at 0.3. For training on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B are conducted on 4×L40 GPUs, and those with Qwen2.5-7B on 4×H20 GPUs. Each model is trained for 1 epoch (500 samples) with 125 iterations.

Appendix C Prompt

C.1 Prompt Details for Training

System Prompt

System prompt is crucial for prompt engineering. The LLM follows the instructions and assumes the role specified in the it, such as translator, programmer, etc. Therefore, as illustrated in Figure 11, we have provided a detailed description of the desired behaviors of the parallel agent within the system prompt to facilitate its parallel exploration and thereby accomplish the task better. Specifically, similar to ReAct, parallel agent is required to engage in reasoning before making a decision. For example, it needs to consider which actions can be executed in parallel to gather more information and which environments warrant further exploration. This reasoning process must be enclosed within the <think></think> tags. After reasoning, the agent can take actions. Unlike ReAct, the parallel agent can interact with multiple environments simultaneously. Thus, we require it to specify environment-specific actions within <parallel></parallel> tags, with each individual action wrapped in <env_i><env> tags to clearly indicate which environment the action belongs to and to enable easier parsing of the actions.

Prompt for First Step

At the beginning of a task, the agent has not yet interacted with the environment. The environment provides only initial state information, a set of available actions, and the task description. We organize this information into a concise yet clear prompt (As shown in Figure 12) to help the agent understand the initial context. Additionally, for ALF-World, we do not include explanations for the available actions. However, for the ScienceWorld dataset, which involves combinations of actions and objects, we introduce brief action descriptions to avoid excessive token consumption.

Prompt for Intermediate Step

As the number of parallel agent exploration steps increases, maintaining the full history of interactions becomes costly in terms of both memory and computation. To address this, at step tt, for information from steps 11 to t−2t-2, we retain only the actions and their corresponding observations within {history_info}. In contrast, for the immediate previous step t−1t-1, we preserve all of the parallel actions, observations, and executable actions within {last_history}. The details of {history_info} and {last_history} are presented in Figure 14 and Figure 15. With this carefully designed prompt presented in Figure 13, the context length is reduced while still retaining sufficient information for the agent to perform its task more effectively.

Exploration-limiting prompt

For experiments that require controlling the number of parallel environments, we designed a prompt to limit the maximum number of environments the model can explore. In this prompt, we specify the allowed number of environments using “env_num” and inform the model that if it attempts to explore more than this number, the entire task will be considered a failure. In addition to this prompt-based restriction, we also enforce behavioral constraints: if the model tries to access an environment that is not permitted, the entire task is immediately seen as failed.

Action-Explanation Prompt

Since the tasks in ScienceWorld require actions to interact with objects and involves a large number of both actions and objects, it is impractical to include all possible object-action combinations in the limited context. Therefore, we adopt the same prompt as RLVMR, which provides only a list of executable actions along with explanations of their specific details and the objects they can interact with. This prompt is illustrated in Figure 17.

C.2 Effectiveness of Designed Prompts

Token Budget Analysis

When tackling long-horizon tasks, traditional methods typically append all historical information and intermediate reasoning steps into a single context window. However, as the number of steps increases, the context continuously expands. In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of our designed prompt in compressing the context window. As illustrated in Figure 10, our method can compress prompts that originally contain at most 50,000 tokens down to at most 7,000 tokens, significantly reducing the token budget while still maintaining the agent’s strong performance.

Comparison of Context Management Strategies

GiGPO employs a similar prompting strategy, but instead of retaining all historical information, it only preserves the most recent few steps within a limited context window. We evaluate GiGPO’s performance with varying context window sizes, as shown in Table 8. Although the context length may be shorter, its performance does not improve as the context window expands. Furthermore, once the number of retained steps exceeds 16, the total context length will surpasses the model’s maximum sequence length, leading to truncation.

In contrast, our proposed prompting design not only preserves more comprehensive historical information but also adheres to the token budget. Furthermore, as demonstrated in Section 5.2 and Section 5.5, under our prompting scheme, the performance of our method consistently improves as the number of environments increases, highlighting its efficiency, robustness and scalability.
